title: Interrupt Priority: Software Polling, Daisy Chain, Parallel Encoder
quickIdea: When several devices can interrupt at once, something must choose. Three standard answers: software polling of status bits, a daisy chain that passes the acknowledge along a wire, and a parallel priority encoder with one request bit per device.
remember: Daisy chain: one common request line, one acknowledge line wired from device to device; the first device in the chain that is requesting blocks the acknowledge and takes the interrupt, so priority is positional and non-uniform.
Software polling: the CPU reads the devices' status registers in a fixed order, so priority is the order written in the program.
Parallel (encoded) priority: each device has its own request bit and a priority encoder produces the winning device's identity, which is the fastest and the most hardware.

Maskable interrupts can be disabled by software (a bit in the control register or the status word); non-maskable ones, such as power failure or an overheating CPU, cannot, because they report conditions that cannot wait.
Highest priority goes to requests that are most damaging to delay: in GATE CSE 2011 Q.11, the CPU temperature sensor outranks the disk, the mouse and the keyboard.

example.prompt: Devices A, B and C are chained in that order, A nearest the CPU. A and C request at the same time. Who is served, and what does C do meanwhile?
example.work: The acknowledge signal reaches A first. A is requesting, so it blocks the signal from passing to B and C, and places its own vector on the bus. C's request line stays asserted but its acknowledge never arrives, so C waits until A's routine finishes and the CPU acknowledges again.
example.answer: A is served first, unconditionally, because priority here is position in the chain - C waits even though its data may be more urgent.

gateAngle: Three questions rotate around this card: 1996 Q.1.24 (daisy chain gives non-uniform priority), 2011 Q.11 (which source deserves the highest priority) and 2020 Q.3 (daisy chaining assigns priorities - true; vectored interrupts need polling - false). All three are one-mark statement questions, so the value is in the vocabulary, not the arithmetic.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 1996 Q.1.24: for the daisy chain scheme, which statement is true - non-uniform priority, uniform priority, only for slow devices, or a separate interrupt pin per device?
variations.answer: It gives non-uniform priority to the various devices.
variations.why: The chain makes priority depend on position, and all devices share one request pin, so the other three options fail.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2020 Q.3: which of the four statements are true - daisy chaining assigns priorities; a vectored interrupt needs CPU polling; polling checks status bits periodically; CPU and DMA can both be bus masters at once?
variations.answer: The first and the third only.
variations.why: A vectored interrupt delivers the vector, so no polling is needed, and bus mastership is exclusive, so the CPU and the controller cannot both be masters.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is a non-maskable interrupt needed at all, if the mask bit already lets software choose which devices to hear?
variations.answer: Because the mask is under software control, and the condition that matters most - power failing, the CPU overheating - must be heard even when software is in the middle of a section with interrupts disabled. A non-maskable line bypasses the mask.
variations.why: It is the reasoning behind 2011 Q.11's answer.

trap.what: Assuming a daisy chain gives all devices equal priority, or that polling and daisy chaining are the same mechanism.
trap.why: The chain is an ordering, so it is non-uniform by construction: the device nearest the CPU wins. And polling is the CPU reading status registers, while the chain resolves the choice in hardware without the CPU reading anything.
trap.counterexample: Swap two devices in the chain and the winner of a simultaneous request changes, though no software changed at all - that alone shows priority is positional, not uniform.

check.question: Two devices request at the same instant. In a parallel priority encoder system, who is served, and how is that different from the daisy chain?
check.answer: The encoder's highest-priority requesting input wins, decided by the encoder's wiring, not by position on a wire; the daisy chain's winner depends on physical position in the chain.
check.explanation: Both give fixed non-uniform priority, but the encoder resolves it in one gate delay and also supplies the device identity.
